title: Nucleic acids
summary: How DNA and RNA are built from nucleotides, why complementary base pairing lets genetic information be copied and expressed, and why a shared genetic code points to a common ancestor of all life.

keyterms.definition: The monomer of nucleic acids, made of a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.
The chain of alternating pentose sugars and phosphate groups, linked covalently, that forms the strand of DNA or RNA with bases projecting from it.
A reaction joining two molecules with the removal of water; links the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next.
Specific pairing of bases by hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine (or uracil in RNA) and cytosine with guanine.
The two strands of a DNA double helix run in opposite directions.
The structure of DNA: two antiparallel polynucleotide strands linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases and wound into a helix.
The pentose sugar in DNA nucleotides; it has one fewer oxygen atom than ribose.
The pentose sugar in RNA nucleotides.
The base found in RNA in place of thymine; it pairs with adenine.
The same codons specify the same amino acids in almost all organisms, which is evidence of universal common ancestry.
Each nucleic acid strand has a 5′ end (phosphate on carbon 5′) and a 3′ end (hydroxyl on carbon 3′); nucleotides are added to the 3′ end.
A base with a double-ring structure: adenine and guanine.
A base with a single-ring structure: cytosine, thymine and uracil.
DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins, held by a further histone attached to linker DNA; it packages eukaryotic DNA.
Experiment using bacteriophages labelled with radioactive 35S (protein) and 32P (DNA), showing DNA, not protein, enters bacteria and is the genetic material.
In DNA from diverse organisms, amount of A equals T and amount of C equals G, so purines equal pyrimidines; this falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis.

lessons.title: Nucleotides and the structure of DNA

questions.prompt: What are the three components of a nucleotide?
options: Amino acid, phosphate and base
Pentose sugar, phosphate and nitrogenous base
Glucose, phosphate and nitrogenous base
Pentose sugar, fatty acid and base
questions.explanation: Every nucleotide contains a five-carbon (pentose) sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. Glucose is a hexose, and amino acids are protein monomers.

questions.statement: DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms.
questions.explanation: All cellular organisms use DNA as their genetic material. Some viruses use RNA instead, but viruses are not considered living organisms.

questions.text: Nucleotides are linked into a strand by ___ reactions, which release water.
questions.explanation: A condensation reaction forms a covalent bond between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next, removing a water molecule. Hydrolysis is the reverse.

questions.prompt: Which part of a nucleic acid strand carries the genetic information?
options: The sequence of phosphate groups
The sequence of pentose sugars
The hydrogen bonds between strands
The sequence of bases
questions.explanation: The sugar–phosphate backbone is identical along the strand; only the order of bases varies, so the base sequence forms the code.

questions.prompt: Match each base to its pairing partner in DNA.
questions.explanation: Complementary base pairing in DNA is always A–T and C–G, held by hydrogen bonds.

questions.statement: The two strands of DNA are held together by covalent bonds between bases.
questions.explanation: The two strands are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. Covalent bonds join sugars and phosphates within each strand.

questions.text: The two strands of a DNA double helix run in opposite directions, so they are described as ___.
questions.explanation: Antiparallel means the strands run in opposite directions. Complementary refers to the base pairing between them.

questions.prompt: In a DNA strand, which atoms or groups are directly linked by covalent bonds in the backbone?
options: The phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next
The base of one nucleotide and the base of the next
The base of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next
The sugar of one nucleotide and the base of the next
questions.explanation: The backbone is alternating sugar and phosphate. Bases are attached to the sugars and project inwards; they are not linked to each other along a strand.

questions.prompt: Order the levels of DNA structure from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: A base is one component of a nucleotide; nucleotides condense into a strand; two antiparallel strands form the double helix.

questions.prompt: A DNA sample contains 30% adenine. What percentage is cytosine?
questions.explanation: A pairs with T, so T = 30% and A + T = 60%. The remaining 40% is split equally between C and G, so C = 20%.

lessons.title: DNA, RNA and the genetic code

questions.prompt: Which row correctly distinguishes RNA from DNA?
options: RNA: double-stranded, deoxyribose, thymine
RNA: single-stranded, ribose, uracil
RNA: single-stranded, deoxyribose, uracil
RNA: double-stranded, ribose, thymine
questions.explanation: RNA is usually a single strand, contains ribose rather than deoxyribose, and has uracil instead of thymine.
RNA has no thymine; uracil takes its place and pairs with adenine, e.g. between mRNA codons and tRNA anticodons.

questions.statement: RNA is a polymer formed by condensation of nucleotide monomers.
questions.explanation: Like DNA, RNA is a polynucleotide built by condensation reactions linking sugar and phosphate to form a backbone.

questions.prompt: How does complementary base pairing allow genetic information to be replicated?
options: Each strand acts as a template, and only one base can pair with each base on it
Bases pair randomly, creating variation in each copy
The sugar–phosphate backbone is copied first and then bases are added
Proteins read the base sequence and synthesise new DNA from amino acids
questions.explanation: Because A only pairs with T and C only with G, the base sequence of each strand determines the sequence of the new strand, so copies are accurate.

questions.prompt: Match each feature to DNA or RNA.
questions.explanation: Both nucleic acids contain A, C and G; DNA has thymine and deoxyribose, RNA has uracil and ribose.

questions.prompt: How many different base sequences are possible for a DNA strand 10 nucleotides long?
options: 4¹⁰
questions.explanation: Each position can be any of 4 bases, so there are 4 × 4 × … (10 times) = 4¹⁰ (over a million) sequences. This is why DNA has a virtually limitless capacity to store information.

questions.statement: The genetic code differs completely between bacteria and humans.
questions.explanation: The genetic code is almost universal: the same codons code for the same amino acids in bacteria, plants and animals, with only minor variations.

questions.prompt: Why is the conservation of the genetic code across all life forms evidence of universal common ancestry?
options: Because a shared code is most simply explained by inheritance from a common ancestor
Because the genetic code is chemically the only one possible
Because all organisms have the same genes
Because all organisms have identical base sequences
questions.explanation: The code is arbitrary, so independent origins would be unlikely to arrive at the same code. Inheritance from a single ancestor best explains why it is shared.

questions.text: DNA is wound into a double ___ formed by two antiparallel strands.
questions.explanation: Two strands linked by complementary base pairs twist to form the double helix.

questions.prompt: How does complementary base pairing allow genetic information to be expressed?
options: Amino acids pair directly with DNA bases
Ribosomes copy DNA into new DNA
mRNA is transcribed using DNA as a template, and tRNA anticodons pair with mRNA codons
Proteins are converted back into DNA
questions.explanation: During transcription RNA bases pair with the DNA template; during translation tRNA anticodons pair with mRNA codons, so the base sequence specifies the amino acid sequence.

options: Cytosine and thymine
Adenine and thymine
Adenine and guanine
Guanine and cytosine
questions.explanation: Adenine and guanine are purines with a double-ring structure; cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines with a single ring.

questions.statement: Each base pair in DNA consists of one purine and one pyrimidine, which keeps the width of the helix constant.
questions.explanation: A double-ring purine paired with a single-ring pyrimidine gives every base pair the same length, so the helix has a uniform diameter, contributing to stability.

questions.text: New nucleotides are always added to the ___ end of a growing nucleic acid strand.
questions.explanation: The phosphate of an incoming nucleotide links to the free 3′ hydroxyl on the strand, so synthesis proceeds 5′ to 3′.

questions.prompt: What is at the 5′ end of a DNA strand?
options: A hydroxyl group on carbon 3′ of deoxyribose
A phosphate group attached to carbon 5′ of deoxyribose
A free nitrogenous base
A histone protein
questions.explanation: The 5′ end has a phosphate linked to the 5′ carbon of the terminal sugar; the 3′ end has a free hydroxyl on carbon 3′.

questions.prompt: Which describes the structure of a nucleosome?
options: DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins, with an additional histone holding it, connected by linker DNA
A single histone wrapped around a loop of RNA
Eight DNA molecules wrapped around one histone
A ring of naked DNA found in prokaryotes
questions.explanation: A nucleosome has DNA coiled around an octamer of histones, secured by a further histone (H1) attached to linker DNA. Prokaryotic DNA is naked.

questions.prompt: Match each Hershey–Chase label to what it marked.
questions.explanation: Proteins contain sulfur but DNA does not; DNA contains phosphorus. Only 32P entered the bacteria, so DNA is the genetic material.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Hershey–Chase experiment.
items: Grow phages with 35S or 32P to label protein or DNA
Allow labelled phages to infect bacteria
Agitate in a blender to detach phage coats
Centrifuge so bacteria form a pellet
Measure radioactivity in the pellet and the supernatant
questions.explanation: After centrifugation, 32P was found in the bacterial pellet while 35S stayed in the supernatant with the empty coats, showing DNA entered the cells.

questions.statement: Chargaff found that the amounts of the four bases are equal in DNA from all organisms.
questions.explanation: Base proportions vary between species. Chargaff found A = T and C = G in each species, which falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis that all four bases repeat in equal amounts.

questions.prompt: Which hypothesis was falsified by Chargaff's data?
options: The hypothesis that DNA is double-stranded
The hypothesis that proteins are made of amino acids
The hypothesis that DNA is replicated semi-conservatively
The tetranucleotide hypothesis, that DNA is a repeating unit of the four bases in equal amounts
questions.explanation: If DNA were repeats of four bases in equal amounts, all species would have 25% of each base. Chargaff's data showed variation between species, so DNA could carry varied information.

questions.text: The bases cytosine, thymine and uracil, which have a single ring, are called ___.
questions.explanation: Pyrimidines have a single ring; purines (A and G) have a double ring.
